newsitem.title: JAPAN: Glencore, China crack Japan's clubby zinc market.
newsitem.headline: Glencore, China crack Japan's clubby zinc market.

text.p: Swiss trade house Glencore and Chinese smelters are cracking Japan's clubby zinc market, with low-priced metal that is increasingly attractive as domestic users struggle with tough global competition, traders say.
"Glencore's offers have always been much lower than others," said Yasuo Odajima, an official at Yodogawa Steel Works Ltd, Japan's largest independent manufacturer of surface-treated steel sheets.
A window of opportunity opened for zinc importers in the past few years when two domestic zinc refineries shut down after a strong yen undermined their competitiveness.

Japan's zinc imports jumped to 112,300 tonnes in 1995 from 72,100 tonnes the year before, despite a drop in domestic demand to 767,300 tonnes from 782,200 as many zinc-consuming manufacturers moved production overseas.
Glencore pounced on the opportunity, while Chinese mines and smelters have also been eager to boost exports to earn hard currency.
"Glencore's Chinese zinc business in Asia has expanded rapidly over the last few years," one industry source said.

Officials at Glencore Far East AG, the Tokyo unit of the Swiss commodity trader, would not comment on their zinc business in Japan, where the market has traditionally been dominated by domestic producers.

Yet official data show Japan's zinc imports from China under a special tariff exemption scheme in April jumped 83.5 percent from the previous year to 89,669 tonnes, equivalent to 79.6 percent of total zinc imports that month.

Traders say China has been selling its zinc particularly agressively after the metal's price rose above $1,250 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange (LME). Chinese producers are even foregoing their usual premium to LME prices, satisfied with the fat profits from the firm global prices.

At the same time, Glencore has been emerging as a big player in the global zinc market after recently purchasing stakes in a number of mining and refining groups, including France's Metaleurop SA, Spain's Asturiana de Zinc SA and Peru's Iscaycruz SA.
In Japan, the trade house has been doing more than just offering low prices to attract customers.
One industry source said that, to promote use of Chinese zinc in Japan, Glencore has sold small lots of Chinese metal for trial use. It has also built up stocks so it can guarantee regular shipments.
"At times when Glencore did not have enough Chinese metal, it has even bought expensive domestic product for delivery to its customers," the source said.
For Japanese steelmakers, who face the threat of competition from foreign imports, lower prices are particularly attractive.
Steelmakers use zinc to make rust-resistant galvanised steel sheet, accounting for about two-thirds of zinc demand.

"(The steel makers') customers, such as car makers, would not easily accept a price hike," said Minoru Hasegawa, mining analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "No matter how domestic producers and traders resist, once an opening appears, it only grows. The same thing has already happened with Korean steel."

An official at another major Japanese zinc consumer said his company was also using Chinese zinc on a trial basis, although it did not want to upset domestic suppliers and had no intention of boosting its use of imports in the near future.

"We are in a dilemma," he said. "While the international zinc prise has risen, we can't roll over the higher production costs to our customers who also face international competition. We don't know what to do."
Glencore's aggressive moves in the Japanese market have ruffled feathers at domestic trade houses and smelting firms.
"I don't know how Glencore can offer such (low) prices," said one executive at a Japanese smelter.
"But in the long term we're not worried. I can't imagine China remaining a zinc exporter beyond the next five years, so we are thinking of raising domestic production again."
